chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
On 9 May 2024, Oklo Inc. completed its merger with AltC Acquisition Corp and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker OKLO, becoming the principal SPAC-listed pure-play available on the thesis that the AI data-centre build-out would require large-scale new nuclear generation capacity at scale. The post-merger entity carried an implied valuation of approximately $850 million at closing. AltC had been sponsored by Sam Altman, the OpenAI chief executive, who served as AltC's chairman and whose involvement gave the transaction an attention-multiplier that few comparable advanced-reactor vehicles could replicate.

## Founders and Technology

Oklo was founded in 2013 by Jacob DeWitte and Caroline Cochran, both MIT nuclear engineering PhDs. The company is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, with DeWitte as CEO and Cochran as COO. Their technology thesis drew on the Experimental Breeder Reactor II heritage at Idaho National Laboratory.

The Aurora powerhouse commercialises that heritage through a compact sodium-cooled fast-spectrum core fuelled by high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) combined with recycled spent fuel. Three plant configurations span 15 MW, 50 MW, and 75 MW, targeting distributed deployment at remote industrial sites, military installations, and data-centre campuses.

## Customer Pipeline

The commercial case for Oklo crystallised through a sequence of escalating customer commitments. In 2023, global data-centre colocation operator [Equinix signed a letter of intent](https://oklo.com/newsroom/news-details/2024/Oklo-Secures-Partnerships-for-Up-to-750-Megawatts-of-Power-for-U.S.-Data-Centers/default.aspx) for 500 MW of Aurora capacity — the largest single data-centre SMR LOI in the industry at the time. The pipeline broadened in 2024 as Oklo announced additional LOIs with Wyoming Hyperscale (100 MW), Diamondback Energy (50 MW for Permian Basin operations), and the US Air Force's Eielson facility in Alaska, which was selected through a DoD demonstration process. Two further unnamed data-centre counterparties added approximately 750 MW, pushing cumulative pipeline past 2,100 MW.

The inflection came in December 2024. On 18 December, Oklo announced a Master Power Agreement with Switch, the data-centre developer, for a [non-binding framework to deploy 12 GW of Aurora powerhouses through 2044](https://www.powermag.com/another-big-data-center-win-for-nuclear-oklo-and-switch-sign-historic-12-gw-deal/), the largest advanced-reactor supply commitment yet announced in the industry. "Rob Roy and the Switch team share the vision we have for nuclear energy's role in powering artificial intelligence," DeWitte said. Switch CEO Rob Roy characterised the arrangement as "a commitment to deploying advanced nuclear power at a transformative scale."

On 9 January 2026, Oklo and Meta Platforms announced a prepayment agreement under which Meta would provide upfront funding to advance a [1.2 GW nuclear power campus in Pike County, Ohio](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260109127781/en/Oklo-Meta-Announce-Agreement-in-Support-of-1.2-GW-Nuclear-Energy-Development-in-Southern-Ohio) — on 206 acres of the former Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant site, a property once owned by the Department of Energy. Oklo would use Meta's funding to secure nuclear fuel and advance Phase 1 engineering. Phase 1 was targeted to come online as early as 2030; full 1.2 GW capacity by 2034.

> "Meta's funding commitment in support of early procurement and activity is a major step in moving advanced nuclear forward," DeWitte said on the announcement.

By the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, Oklo's non-binding order pipeline had grown to approximately 14 GW from a standing start below 1 GW in mid-2023.

## Financial Baseline

The SPAC merger delivered approximately $306 million in net cash at close. Oklo remained pre-revenue through the post-merger period, with operating losses reflecting R&D expenditure and NRC licensing activities. The company executed an at-the-market equity programme through late 2025 and into Q1 2026, issuing approximately 12.4 million shares for net proceeds of roughly $1.18 billion. As of [31 March 2026, the balance sheet carried $2.54 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and marketable debt securities](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/oklo-inc-oklo-q1-2026-050034149.html) against modest liabilities of $64.9 million, extending its operating runway substantially. The Q1 2026 net loss was $33.1 million, against $9.8 million for the same period a year prior, as R&D and general and administrative costs scaled with the licensing programme.

## NRC Licensing Trajectory

The regulatory pathway advanced in two notable steps through 2025. On 17 July, Oklo announced that the [NRC had completed a pre-application readiness assessment](https://oklo.com/newsroom/news-details/2025/Oklo-Advances-Licensing-with-Completion-of-NRC-Readiness-Assessment/default.aspx) for Phase 1 of the combined licence application for the Aurora-INL plant, identifying no significant gaps.

> "We view this assessment as a productive engagement tool that moves our licensing and permitting work forward," DeWitte said.

On 30 September, the NRC accepted Oklo's Principal Design Criteria topical report under an [accelerated review timeline](https://oklo.com/newsroom/news-details/2025/Oklos-NRC-Principal-Design-Criteria-Topical-Report-Accepted-for-Review-Under-an-Accelerated-Timeline/default.aspx), with an acceptance notice issued in 15 days against a typical 30–60-day window, and a draft evaluation expected in early 2026 at less than half the traditional review schedule. Oklo stated its intention to submit the Phase 1 COLA before year-end 2025. Altman stepped down from the board chairmanship in approximately April 2025 amid the increasingly complex OpenAI conflict-of-interest dynamics as AI compute demand converged on nuclear power supply; Lieutenant General John Jansen, USAF (retired), succeeded him as chairman.

## The Central Tension

The dossier that follows traces the binary structure of the Oklo investment. The equity traded, as of the snapshot date, on a pipeline of non-binding commitments and licensing milestones rather than revenue, construction permits, or operating assets. Converting the Switch and Meta frameworks into binding power purchase agreements, securing a commercial HALEU fuel supply in a domestic enrichment market structurally constrained by the 2023 Russian uranium import ban, and obtaining NRC licence approval for a sodium-cooled fast-spectrum design without modern US commercial precedent represented the three inter-dependent execution risks the company had to resolve before Aurora could be declared commercial. How those risks compare to the trajectories of NuScale, X-energy, TerraPower, Kairos Power, and BWXT defines the competitive context that the subsequent chapters examine.

chapters.title: From 2013 MIT founding to the AltC SPAC merger
chapters.body:
## The Founders and the Fast Reactor

Jacob DeWitte and Caroline Cochran met inside the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's nuclear science and engineering programme, where both were pursuing doctoral degrees. In 2013, before either had completed their PhDs, they incorporated Oklo Inc. and staked the company on a reactor concept that the American commercial nuclear industry had largely set aside since the Cold War: the sodium-cooled fast reactor.

The design lineage ran to the Experimental Breeder Reactor II — EBR-II — a sodium-cooled, metallic-fuel fast reactor that operated at what is now Idaho National Laboratory from 1964 until its congressionally mandated shutdown in 1994. Over three decades of operation, EBR-II had demonstrated passive safety characteristics, an ability to consume its own spent fuel, and an operational reliability record that its advocates regarded as an unfinished proof of concept. DeWitte, who had completed his undergraduate degree in nuclear engineering at the University of Florida before arriving at MIT, absorbed that heritage in his doctoral research. He and Cochran saw in it the foundation for a compact, factory-manufacturable reactor plant that could be deployed at remote industrial sites far outside the reach of the existing transmission grid.

The company entered Y Combinator in 2014, an unusual credential for a deep-technology nuclear startup and an early signal of the Silicon Valley adjacency that would later define the Altman chapter of the Oklo story. The Aurora powerhouse — as the reactor plant design came to be called — was configured for outputs ranging from 15 megawatts to 75 megawatts, dimensions chosen to fit within the footprint and capital budgets of off-grid industrial facilities. The reactor would use metallic uranium fuel, a form closer to EBR-II's heritage than the ceramic fuel pellets common in conventional light-water reactors, and would be capable in principle of consuming recycled spent nuclear fuel as a feedstock — a feature with significant long-term fuel-cycle implications that Oklo repeatedly cited as a differentiator.

## The NRC Application and the 2022 Denial

Oklo's regulatory engagement with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission began well before any formal licence submission. The company initiated pre-application meetings with NRC staff under the agency's advanced reactor framework, accumulating years of technical exchange on the Aurora design's novel characteristics. In parallel, the Department of Energy granted Oklo a site use permit at Idaho National Laboratory — the same site where EBR-II had operated — for a planned Aurora demonstration plant.

In March 2020, Oklo submitted a combined licence application to the NRC for the INL Aurora plant, the first combined licence application for an advanced non-light-water reactor in the agency's history. The submission was a milestone in form; the substance, however, exposed the limits of an early-stage application from a company with a small engineering organisation. In January 2022, the NRC's Atomic Safety and Licensing Board denied the application without prejudice, citing inadequate information across several technical areas: the application had not sufficiently addressed the classification of safety-significant structures, systems, and components; the treatment of accident source terms and radiological consequence analysis was incomplete; and the probabilistic risk assessment methodology had not been developed to the level of detail the staff required for a combined licence review. The denial was not a rejection on the merits of the Aurora concept; it was a procedural determination that the application as filed could not support the rigorous safety review the agency's regulations required.

The "without prejudice" designation preserved Oklo's right to resubmit, and the company said publicly that it would do so with a more complete application. The episode nonetheless established a recurring theme in the Oklo narrative: the distance between a technically credible reactor concept and the evidentiary standard required for NRC approval of a novel reactor design. Oklo submitted a revised combined licence application for the INL Aurora plant in late 2023, restarting the formal review process with an application the company characterised as substantially more detailed.

## Sam Altman, AltC, and the SPAC Transaction

The broader narrative around Oklo shifted in July 2023, when the company announced a business combination with AltC Acquisition Corp, a special-purpose acquisition company whose chairman was Sam Altman. Altman had been an investor in and informal adviser to Oklo for years before the AltC transaction — a relationship that reflected his longstanding view that artificial intelligence's electricity demands would eventually exhaust conventional generation capacity and require a new class of always-on, low-carbon power. As CEO of OpenAI, Altman was simultaneously building the organisation whose compute infrastructure would most directly embody that thesis.

AltC had raised $450 million in its IPO on the strength of Altman's sponsorship, a figure that reflected investor appetite to participate in whatever Altman chose to back in the energy transition. The announced merger terms implied a post-combination enterprise value of approximately $850 million for Oklo — a valuation based almost entirely on the company's technology promise, its customer letter-of-intent pipeline, and the Altman association, given that Oklo had not yet recognised a dollar of revenue.

The transaction closed on May 9, 2024, listing Oklo on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker OKLO. The post-merger balance sheet carried approximately $306 million in cash. Altman continued as chairman of the Oklo board following the merger, a governance signal the market interpreted as a sustained endorsement rather than a transactional exit.

> "We believe advanced fission can play an important role in addressing the energy needs of the future," DeWitte said at the time of the merger announcement, "and this business combination gives us the resources and visibility to execute on that mission."

## Post-Merger Commercialisation and the Pipeline

The public listing accelerated Oklo's commercial development activity in ways the private phase had not. The Equinix, Switch, Diamondback Energy, and Eielson Air Force Base letters of intent collectively assembled a forward customer pipeline in the gigawatts.

The NRC review of the revised combined licence application for the INL Aurora plant remained the governing constraint on the commercialisation timeline. Oklo's re-submitted application entered the NRC's formal acceptance review process; the agency's combined licence review, under normal sequencing, takes several years from acceptance to issuance — a timeline that placed any initial commercial operation date well into the late 2020s at the earliest, contingent on a review process for a reactor type the NRC had never before licensed to operate.

In April 2025, Sam Altman stepped down as chairman, succeeded by Lieutenant General John Jansen (USAF, retired). The transition was characterised as planned succession driven by OpenAI conflict-of-interest considerations.

## Twelve Years and a Blank Income Statement

What the 2013-to-2026 arc produced was singular in the US nuclear industry: a listed equity, traded on the NYSE, with a chairman succession from Sam Altman to a retired Air Force general, a customer LOI pipeline denominated in hundreds of megawatts, and a balance sheet carrying over $300 million in post-SPAC cash — all without a single dollar of commercial revenue, a granted construction permit, or a shovel in the ground at any site.

Oklo remained, as of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, a pre-revenue, pre-permit, pre-construction enterprise. What 12 years of founder-led development had produced was not a reactor but a regulatory position, a customer pipeline, and a market narrative: the principal pure-play SMR equity available to investors seeking exposure to the AI data centre electricity demand thesis, sponsored by the most prominent technology investor in the United States, and built on reactor physics that the Department of Energy had validated at Idaho decades before Jacob DeWitte and Caroline Cochran had enrolled at MIT.

chapters.title: The Aurora powerhouse, fuel recycling, and the customer engagement model
chapters.body:
## The reactor at the core

The Aurora powerhouse is Oklo's commercial answer to a challenge that has occupied nuclear engineers since the 1960s: extracting maximum energy from uranium while operating safely without active cooling systems, at a scale compact enough to fit inside an industrial warehouse. The machine Oklo is working to license is a compact fast-spectrum sodium-cooled reactor fuelled by metallic uranium alloy, targeting electrical output across three configurations — 15 megawatts for the demonstration unit at Idaho National Laboratory, 50 megawatts, and 75 megawatts for larger commercial deployments — depending on customer power requirements and site constraints. At the upper end of that range, a single Aurora unit could supply a mid-scale hyperscale data centre campus with dispatchable, carbon-free baseload power continuously. A cluster of 75 MW units underpins the multi-hundred-megawatt commitments Oklo had assembled in its letter-of-intent pipeline by the time of the frozen snapshot date.

## Heritage and passive safety: the EBR-II legacy

Oklo's engineers were not designing in a vacuum. When the founders drew on DOE heritage, they were building on proven physics. The Aurora's direct technical ancestor is the [Experimental Breeder Reactor II](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/5-fast-facts-about-experimental-breeder-reactor-ii), which operated at Idaho National Laboratory from 1965 to 1994 — a span of nearly three decades during which it generated roughly 2.1 terawatt-hours of electricity and, more importantly, proved several foundational principles that Oklo carried forward into its commercial design.

EBR-II was a sodium-cooled fast reactor burning metallic fuel — an alloy of uranium and zirconium — rather than the ceramic uranium dioxide pellets used in conventional light-water reactors. Fast-spectrum neutrons interact with the fuel differently from the thermalised neutrons in a light-water machine, enabling higher fuel utilisation and, in breeder configurations, the generation of additional fissile material from fertile uranium-238. The combination of fast-spectrum physics and metallic fuel also yields a particular safety characteristic: as the reactor heats up, its reactivity drops naturally through an effect known as a negative temperature coefficient. The fuel expands, neutrons escape, and the fission chain reaction throttles itself without any operator action or active safety system intervention.

That property was demonstrated empirically in April 1986, when engineers at Argonne National Laboratory — which managed EBR-II — conducted landmark passive-safety tests. They deliberately switched off the primary coolant pumps with the reactor at full power, simulating the loss-of-flow accident scenario that had defined light-water reactor risk since Three Mile Island, and then simply watched. EBR-II coasted to a safe shutdown temperature entirely through its own physics, with no operator action and no engineered safety actuation. A second test the same day replicated the result for an unprotected loss-of-heat-sink scenario. Both results were published and remain foundational citations in the case for metallic-fuelled sodium-cooled reactors. Aurora inherits that physics directly.

The DOE shut EBR-II down in 1994 under congressional pressure during post-Cold War budget contraction and a broader US retreat from fast-reactor development. DeWitte and Cochran, who met while studying nuclear engineering at MIT, viewed that discontinuity not as a closed chapter but as unfinished work — a proven machine set aside before commercialisation. Idaho National Laboratory retained the institutional knowledge, the experimental record, and, critically, the site. Oklo's subsequent site use agreement with DOE, granting access to INL for the Aurora demonstration plant, put the company back at the location where EBR-II had run for nearly three decades.

## HALEU and the fuel-cycle distinction

Aurora's fuel specification sets it apart from most other advanced reactor developers and introduces a supply-chain constraint that shapes Oklo's competitive position. The reactor requires [high-assay low-enriched uranium](https://www.energy.gov/ne/nuclear-reactor-technologies/advanced-reactor-technologies/high-assay-low-enriched-uranium-haleu) — HALEU — enriched to between roughly five and 19.75 percent uranium-235 by weight. Conventional light-water reactor fuel is enriched to between three and five percent; HALEU's elevated assay allows smaller, more compact reactor cores with higher power density and extended refuelling intervals, but it cannot be produced by the standard commercial enrichment infrastructure that supplies the existing global reactor fleet.

[Centrus Energy](https://www.centrusenergy.com/) is currently the only US company licensed to produce HALEU at commercial scale, operating a demonstration cascade of advanced centrifuges at its Piketon, Ohio facility under a DOE contract. [Urenco USA](https://www.urenco.com/about-urenco/urenco-usa) at its New Mexico facility had announced plans to add HALEU production capacity, and the DOE funded additional enrichment development under the HALEU Availability Program. But domestic HALEU production as of the snapshot date remained far below what a scaled deployment of advanced reactors would require, and the 2022 congressional ban on Russian uranium imports — cutting off TENEX supply that had backstopped US enrichment for years — had not yet been fully compensated by alternative domestic capacity.

Oklo's partial answer to the HALEU constraint is fuel recycling. The Aurora's fast-spectrum neutron environment enables the reactor to burn not only fresh HALEU but also recycled metallic fuel derived from used nuclear material — a capability that, in principle, extends the effective fuel supply and reduces long-term waste volumes. The company had described its fuel strategy in terms of a closed fuel cycle model; the longer-term vision involves co-locating fuel recycling capability with Aurora deployments, though that element of the business remained in earlier development stages relative to the reactor licensing effort itself.

## The owner-operator PPA model

Oklo's commercial architecture departed sharply from the conventional nuclear industry model, in which reactor vendors sell equipment and engineering services to utility customers who own, operate, and bear the operating cost risk of the plants. Oklo intended to own and operate its Aurora plants itself, selling electricity output under long-term power purchase agreements — PPAs — to end customers. The distinction matters enormously for how risk and return are allocated.

Under a traditional vendor model, the customer absorbs construction cost overruns, fuel procurement volatility, and operating expenses. Under Oklo's PPA model, the customer buys a fixed or indexed electricity price for a defined contract term — structurally similar to a renewable energy offtake agreement — while Oklo retained asset ownership and operational responsibility. For data centre operators managing multi-year power procurement commitments against capital expenditure that increasingly ran to billions of dollars per campus, the structure offered cost predictability and carbon accounting clarity. For Oklo, it implied a capital-intensive balance sheet as plants were built and commissioned, but also a recurring revenue stream once the fleet was operating — resembling an independent power producer more than a technology licensor. The model was explicitly modelled on a capital-recycling logic: own the first plants, demonstrate economics, then refinance or sell down assets to fund successive builds.

## Customer pipeline and LOI structure

Oklo had assembled a pipeline of letters of intent covering more than 750 megawatts of potential capacity by the time the AltC SPAC merger closed in May 2024, spanning data centre operators, energy companies, and the US Department of Defense.

Equinix signed an LOI for 500 megawatts — the single largest commitment in Oklo's pipeline. Switch and the Wyoming Energy Authority also signed LOIs.

Diamondback Energy added an industrial dimension, addressing power-constrained Permian Basin operations.

The DoD selected Oklo for a microreactor demonstration at Eielson Air Force Base in Alaska, validating Aurora as a credible defence energy solution.



## The Idaho demonstration as the proving ground

The Aurora-INL plant — the 15 MW demonstration unit targeted for construction at Idaho National Laboratory — was the linchpin of the entire commercial strategy. It was the first plant for which Oklo submitted a combined license application to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, and its licensing trajectory cascaded directly through the customer LOI pipeline: every downstream commercial deployment was structurally conditional on Oklo demonstrating that it could navigate the NRC process and commission a working reactor.

The NRC initially declined the first combined license application in January 2022; Oklo subsequently engaged in supplemental exchanges and worked toward a revised submission. The licensing timeline directly bounded the realistic commercialisation schedule for the Equinix and Switch LOIs, which could not convert to binding PPAs and construction commitments until the regulatory pathway had demonstrated at least partial resolution and a construction permit was within reach.

The Aurora-INL demonstration was also the vehicle through which Oklo's fuel-recycling capability would be tested at near-commercial scale, closing the loop between the EBR-II experimental heritage at INL, the structural HALEU supply constraint that shaped the fuel cycle strategy, and the long-run owner-operator economics the PPA model depended on. Whether the demonstration plant represented a six-year runway to commercial operation or a longer regulatory journey remained, at the frozen snapshot date, the central question every investor in the thesis was pricing.

chapters.title: Pre-revenue economics, post-SPAC cash, and the LOI-to-revenue path
chapters.body:
## Post-SPAC Balance Sheet: The $306 Million Starting Line

Oklo's path to the public markets culminated on May 9, 2024, when the company completed its business combination with AltC Acquisition Corp. The transaction — sponsored by Sam Altman, who had served as AltC's chairman — delivered approximately $306 million to Oklo's post-merger balance sheet, net of redemptions by AltC public shareholders and transaction costs. Per the company's [8-K and subsequent filings with the SEC](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001849056), the merger implied a post-combination enterprise value of roughly $850 million. That valuation rested entirely on forward expectations: Oklo carried no revenue, no completed Aurora powerhouse, and no issued NRC combined license at closing.

The $306 million positioned the company not as a growth-stage enterprise flush with product receipts but as a regulatory and engineering organisation operating under a multi-year cash deployment plan. The implied cost to reach commercial operation of a first Aurora plant — estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars per unit for first-of-a-kind nuclear construction — meant the SPAC proceeds represented a bridge rather than a destination.

## The Operating Loss Structure

Oklo's cost profile fits the archetype of a pre-construction advanced nuclear developer. Operating expenses fall into three principal categories: research and development activity (encompassing reactor physics, materials qualification, and thermal-hydraulic modelling), general and administrative costs (including the legal and technical work associated with the NRC licensing process and post-SPAC public company obligations), and non-cash stock-based compensation inflated by equity awards granted in connection with the merger transaction.

For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024 — the company's first full year as a listed entity — Oklo's [annual report on Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001849056) reflected operating losses driven by all three categories, with the stock-based compensation charge substantially elevating the reported GAAP net loss above the company's underlying cash consumption. That distinction carries material weight for investors attempting to assess burn rate and runway.

| Expense Category | Cash / Non-Cash | Phase Character |
|---|---|---|
| R&D — engineering, NRC licensing support | Cash | Ongoing; intensifies pre-license |
| G&A — legal, finance, corporate infrastructure | Largely cash | Elevated post-SPAC; normalising |
| Stock-based compensation | Non-cash | Spike at SPAC close; declining |
| Capital expenditure | Minimal | Pre-construction; rises sharply at build |

Cash operating burn — the figure most relevant to runway analysis — reflected salaries and fees for a headcount concentrated in nuclear engineering, regulatory affairs, and materials science, supplemented by direct NRC filing costs and external counsel. The NRC combined license application for the Aurora-INL demonstration unit represented the single largest programmatic expenditure outside of corporate infrastructure. A pre-construction nuclear developer does not pour concrete or purchase turbines in its early public-market years; it retains specialists, assembles technical documentation packages, and sustains a licensing process measured in quarters rather than weeks.

## Cash Position and Runway: Reading the Quarterly Tape

From the approximately $306 million starting position at SPAC close, Oklo's cash balance declined through subsequent quarters as operating expenditures accumulated. The company's [quarterly reports on Form 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001849056) tracked this evolution, and the cash flow statements — particularly the operating cash flow line excluding non-cash items — provided the clearest read on the company's sustainable consumption rate.

At the implied quarterly cash burn rate visible in those statements, the post-SPAC balance was expected to fund pre-construction operations well into the late 2020s before the build-out financing phase would compel fresh capital raises. The company had not issued formal guidance on a specific runway endpoint as of the snapshot date. Analysts covering the advanced nuclear sector, however, had noted the gap between current cash and the capital requirement for Aurora-INL construction with considerable attention.

The critical nuance for a sophisticated investor is the phase discontinuity in capital intensity. Pre-construction burn, dominated by salaries, regulatory fees, and engineering overhead, is an order of magnitude below what arrives when concrete is poured. A first-of-a-kind advanced reactor demonstration plant in the United States — no prior Aurora unit having been built commercially — carries cost uncertainty ranges typical of nuclear firsts: wide, skewed upward, and not fully absorbed by the current balance sheet. The SPAC proceeds funded the licensing work; they do not fund the plant.

## Equity Capital Structure: Founders, Sponsor Shares, and Warrants

Post-merger, Oklo's equity register comprises several distinct layers. The public float derives from former AltC shareholders who did not redeem at merger close, augmented by any PIPE participants who entered through the transaction structure. Founders Jacob DeWitte and Caroline Cochran retained material equity positions; their share holdings, grant schedules, and officer vesting terms were disclosed in the company's proxy statement and Section 16 reports filed with [SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001849056).

Altman's equity exposure attracted the most sustained investor attention. As AltC's sponsor, he held the founder shares characteristic of blank-check company sponsorships — shares acquired at nominal cost and typically subject to forfeiture conditions tied to post-merger share price targets or holding periods. His continued role as Oklo's executive chairman post-merger, disclosed in the company's corporate governance filings, reinforced the signal investors attributed to his involvement beyond the purely financial stake.

The capital structure additionally included publicly listed warrants exercisable into Oklo common shares at $11.50 per share — the standard AltC SPAC warrant feature. These warrants represent incremental dilution upon exercise, a structural feature of SPAC-originated equity registers that investors in de-SPAC names model separately from basic share counts when computing fully diluted economics.

## The LOI Pipeline: Size, Character, and Distance from Revenue

Oklo's investor narrative rested substantially on the volume and provenance of its letters of intent. The Equinix 500 MW LOI and additional counterparties — Switch, Wyoming Energy Authority, Eielson Air Force Base, and Diamondback Energy — collectively ran to gigawatts of potential offtake.

None of it generated revenue as of the snapshot date.

The gap between an LOI and first revenue is structural: an LOI is not a PPA, construction contract, or regulatory authorisation. The sequence from LOI to commercial megawatt-hour spans configuration, environmental review, NRC licence, financing, construction, commissioning, and operating authorisation — a minimum of five years from licence issuance, which remained pending.

Modelling the LOI-to-revenue timeline for a first Aurora unit conservatively produces an eight-to-ten year span from initial customer agreement to first commercial megawatt-hour. The Equinix 500 MW LOI, executed before the NRC application had completed its review cycle and before construction financing was arranged, sits at the leftmost point on that timeline. The investment case demanded patience unusual even by the standards of capital-intensive infrastructure development.

## Capital Allocation in the Pre-Revenue Phase

Oklo's capital deployment in the pre-revenue phase followed a rational hierarchy for a licensing-driven developer. Engineering and physics talent — nuclear engineers, materials scientists, thermal-hydraulics specialists — constituted the most mission-critical spend, sustaining the technical documentation packages that the NRC's combined licence review demands. Legal and regulatory expenditure, covering both the NRC process and the ongoing obligations of a listed company, represented the second largest allocation. External consultants and testing facilities for Aurora fuel cycle and materials work rounded out the material cash items.

Capital expenditure in the conventional sense — physical plant, tooling, site infrastructure — remained minimal through the pre-construction phase. The Idaho National Laboratory site agreement with the Department of Energy provided a designated deployment location for the Aurora demonstration unit, but the physical capital intensity of that deployment did not arrive until after licence issuance and financing close. The current balance sheet was being consumed by people and process, not steel and concrete.

## The Forward Capital Question

Every quarter without an NRC licence or a construction financing close drew the balance sheet incrementally closer to the point where Oklo would return to capital markets in size. The company had not issued explicit guidance on timing or structure for the construction-phase capital raise as of the snapshot date. Advanced nuclear sector analysts had modelled scenarios ranging from a follow-on equity offering in the 2026-2027 window to a structured project finance package underwritten in part by a Department of Energy loan guarantee through the Loan Programs Office — a mechanism that had supported other advanced reactor programmes and for which Oklo's DOE relationship provided institutional standing.

The INL site agreement constituted partial institutional backing, but did not substitute for the capital required to move from blueprint to operating reactor. Aurora's per-unit construction cost estimate ran into the hundreds of millions of dollars.

Investors assessing Oklo's equity confronted a precise version of the pre-revenue nuclear developer's dilemma. The LOI pipeline validated market demand from credible counterparties. The NRC licensing process, however slow, validated technical seriousness and regulatory engagement. The Altman / AltC sponsorship provided access to capital markets at terms unavailable to most advanced nuclear developers. But the cash-to-revenue timeline was measured in years, the construction capital requirement exceeded the current balance sheet, and every assumption in the model rested on NRC milestone timing that the company did not fully control.

The $306 million brought in at the SPAC close was not a solution to the capital problem. It was, precisely, a runway — long enough to reach the licence, short enough to require another act.

chapters.title: Post-SPAC quarterly cadence and the customer pipeline updates
chapters.body:
## The First Earnings Call: Q2 2024

Oklo's first earnings as a listed company followed the May 2024 SPAC close. When DeWitte addressed investors for the first time as chief executive of a listed company — reporting second-quarter 2024 results — the narrative frame he established would define each subsequent quarterly disclosure: Oklo was a licensing and pipeline story, and every milestone that brought the Aurora reactor closer to a combined licence from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission would compress the distance between the current zero-revenue reality and the forward commercial opportunity.

The cash position provided meaningful runway. With operating losses reflecting R&D expenditure and regulatory engagement rather than capital-intensive construction, the quarterly burn rate was manageable against the $306 million starting balance. DeWitte used that first call to anchor investor expectations firmly in the pre-commercial development frame, emphasising the NRC licensing trajectory and the customer pipeline as the two primary variables investors should track quarter to quarter. The balance sheet, he made clear, was not the story — the pipeline was.

## Cash and Operating Losses: A Pre-Revenue Cadence

From Q2 2024 onwards, each quarterly report followed a consistent structural pattern: a cash balance declining at a rate dictated by R&D and overhead expenditure, operating losses consistent with a company still several years from first commercial operation, and a balance sheet that remained the company's principal financial asset. The post-SPAC proceeds established a multi-year runway that insulated the equity narrative from near-term liquidity pressure, allowing management to present each quarter primarily through the lens of operational and regulatory progress rather than financial stress.

| Period | Cash (approx.) | Primary Narrative Anchor |
|---|---|---|
| Q2 2024 | ~$306M at SPAC close | First listed-company quarter; pipeline framing established |
| Q3 2024 | Sequential draw-down | LOI pipeline expansion; NRC request responses |
| Q4 2024 | Sequential draw-down | Full-year 2024 review; AI thesis re-rating in equity |
| Q1 2025 | Sequential draw-down | Board Chairman transition; continued LOI momentum |
| Q2–Q3 2025 | Sequential draw-down | NRC milestone updates; investor day events |
| Q4 2025 / Q1 2026 | Sequential draw-down | Combined licence trajectory; pipeline maturation |

The operating loss trajectory was consistent with comparable pre-commercial advanced reactor companies: heavy on engineering salaries, regulatory engagement costs, and administrative overhead, light on capital expenditure given the absence of active construction. What distinguished Oklo from earlier-stage nuclear startups was the combination of a meaningful cash buffer, DOE site access at INL, and a customer pipeline that gave each quarter a concrete commercial anchor.

## The Customer Pipeline Across Quarters

The Equinix LOI, announced in 2023, gave Oklo a headline customer commitment that signalled hyperscale operators were prepared to make long-horizon nuclear commitments.

Each quarter from Q2 2024 onwards, management updated investors on the pipeline's evolution. Switch, the data centre and technology infrastructure company, featured alongside the Equinix anchor. The US Air Force engagement — smaller in absolute megawatt terms but strategically significant for the defence-sector legitimacy it conferred — received consistent mention as evidence that Oklo's distributed deployment thesis extended beyond the hyperscale market into government and remote-installation use cases.

DeWitte returned, quarter after quarter, to a consistent commercial argument: the scale of electricity demand from AI compute infrastructure had created a structural procurement problem that conventional grid solutions could not resolve on commercially relevant timelines, and Aurora's distributed configuration — ranging from 15 megawatts to 75 megawatts — was sized for siting at individual data centre campuses in ways that gigawatt-class traditional reactors were not. The argument resonated with investors navigating an equity market that had begun pricing AI electricity scarcity as a structural theme rather than a cyclical phenomenon.

The aggregate pipeline, measured by disclosed LOI-stage megawatts, grew across the post-SPAC quarters as the customer roster broadened. Management released updated pipeline figures at investor events and in quarterly earnings materials, framing the expanding total as evidence that the Equinix relationship was proving out a replicable commercial model rather than representing an isolated anomaly.

## The Altman Chairmanship and Its April 2025 Transition

Sam Altman's April 2025 step-down from the chairmanship, succeeded by Lieutenant General John Jansen (USAF, retired), landed in the Q1 2025 reporting window and generated significant market attention.

The equity market's response was watched closely. The AI infrastructure re-rating that had driven a substantial OKLO advance from SPAC-close levels through late 2024 and into 2025 had been materially amplified by the Altman signal; his April 2025 departure represented the first significant test of whether the equity could sustain its re-rated valuation on operational fundamentals alone. That the stock had reached levels far above its initial SPAC reference price reflected not Altman personally but the structural repricing of any credible nuclear generation asset in an environment where AI data centre operators were increasingly explicit about their inability to source sufficient dispatchable carbon-free power from the existing grid.

## NRC Milestones and the Licensing Cadence

Across each quarterly disclosure from Q2 2024 through Q1 2026, the NRC combined licence application trajectory was the operational metric that most directly governed the forward commercial timeline. The NRC review of the resubmitted combined licence application remained the critical-path variable.

Each quarter, management disclosed progress in the NRC review process: responses to requests for additional information, staff review stage completions, and the ongoing DOE Idaho National Laboratory site engagement that would govern the first Aurora deployment. DeWitte consistently presented the NRC timeline as the critical path variable. The customer LOI pipeline carried commercial weight only to the extent that the licensing process resolved within timelines that the LOIs contemplated — a linkage that sophisticated investors tracked across quarters with close attention.

The post-SPAC quarterly cadence, from Q2 2024 through Q1 2026, thus established a consistent investor narrative: a well-capitalised pre-commercial company burning cash at a managed rate, building a customer pipeline with meaningful disclosed commitments, navigating a novel regulatory process without established precedent, and doing so with the founder-CEO in uninterrupted operational command from 2013 through to the frozen snapshot date. The equity's substantial volatility across this period reflected the market's ongoing calibration of the probability-weighted value of that pipeline against a commercial operation date that remained, across every quarterly filing in this window, forward-dated beyond the next reporting horizon.

chapters.title: DeWitte, Cochran, Altman, and the technical-and-investor board
chapters.body:
## The Founders at the Helm

The most enduring fact about Oklo's leadership structure is also the simplest: the two people who filed the first paperwork to incorporate the company in 2013 remained its chief executive and chief operating officer at the time of the company's May 2024 New York Stock Exchange debut and through the frozen-window date of May 23, 2026. That continuity — Jacob DeWitte as CEO, Caroline DeWitte (née Cochran) as COO, occupying the same roles they held as graduate-student co-founders — is unusual for a deep-technology startup that spent more than a decade in pre-revenue development, survived a Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing rejection, executed a SPAC transaction, and built a customer pipeline anchored by some of the largest data-centre operators in the United States. It is also, to sophisticated investors, one of the more legible risk signals the company offers: mission-aligned founder leadership with domain expertise in exactly the technical and regulatory problem that is Oklo's principal challenge.

## Jacob DeWitte: Engineer, Founder, Chairman

Jacob DeWitte turned 40 in the year the 2026 annual meeting proxy was filed. He completed a B.S. in Nuclear Engineering at the University of Florida and a Ph.D. at MIT's Department of Nuclear Science and Engineering (2011–2014), founding Oklo in July 2013 during his doctoral candidacy.

The technical biography runs deeper still. Over a dozen years before founding Oklo, DeWitte served as an intern or fellow at Sandia National Laboratories during the summers of 2002, 2003, 2006, and 2007; at Urenco Limited, the uranium enrichment supplier, in 2005; as a research intern at General Electric in 2008; and as a Visiting Fellow at the United States Naval Nuclear Laboratory in 2009 and 2011. He sat on the board of the American Nuclear Society from 2009 to 2011. By the time he filed Oklo's incorporation documents, DeWitte had accumulated roughly a decade of hands-on exposure across enrichment, utility-scale reactor services, national-laboratory research, and naval nuclear applications — a span that is atypical for founders in the advanced reactor space.

The corporate governance role evolved materially during the twelve months before the snapshot date. Altman's departure from the board on April 22, 2025 left the chairmanship vacant. The board named DeWitte to fill it: per the 2026 annual meeting proxy statement filed with the SEC on April 21, 2026, DeWitte has served as Chairman of the Board since April 2025, combining the chairman and chief executive roles in a single seat. [Oklo Inc. DEF 14A, April 21, 2026, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001849056](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1849056/000184905626000023/a2025proxy.htm)

## Caroline DeWitte: Co-Founder, COO, and Nuclear Engineer

Caroline DeWitte, who was known professionally as Caroline Cochran through Oklo's pre-public period, co-founded the company alongside Jacob DeWitte at Oklo's inception in July 2013. The pair are married to each other, a fact disclosed in both the 2025 and 2026 proxy statements. The co-founder partnership has been a continuous structural feature of the company across its entire operating history.

Her educational profile differs from her co-founder's in a notable way that is often glossed over in shorthand references to Oklo's "two MIT nuclear engineers." DeWitte holds a Master of Science in Nuclear Engineering from MIT — she studied there from 2007 to 2010 — but her undergraduate degrees are a Bachelor of Arts in Economics and a Bachelor of Science in Mechanical Engineering from the University of Oklahoma, where she later received the Regent's Outstanding Alumni Award. Before founding Oklo, she worked as a marketing and engineering consultant from March 2011 to July 2013 and carried policy exposure from a Programs Analysis and Evaluation internship at the Office of the Secretary of Defense in 2005. From 2018 to 2019 she served on the U.S. Department of Energy's Nuclear Energy Advisory Committee and appeared as a panel member at the ninth Clean Energy Ministerial. [Oklo Inc. DEF 14A, April 21, 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1849056/000184905626000023/a2025proxy.htm)

The COO scope across Oklo's pre-commercial period spans customer pipeline management, operational execution, and the regulatory-interface work that runs alongside NRC licensing. As a board director since May 2024, Caroline DeWitte is among the Class II directors standing for re-election at the June 2026 annual meeting.

## The Executive Tier

Beneath the co-founder pair, the executive team was substantially restructured for the public-company phase. R. Craig Bealmear, 59, joined as Chief Financial Officer of Legacy Oklo in August 2023 — roughly nine months before the SPAC merger closed — and has continued in that role post-listing. His prior career was heavily concentrated in hydrocarbon energy finance: he served as Chief Financial Officer of Renewable Energy Group, a biodiesel producer acquired by Chevron Corporation in June 2022, from April 2021 to December 2022; before that, as Chief Financial Officer for North America Downstream at BP plc from March 2015 to December 2020; and before that as Deputy Chief Financial Officer for BP's Refining and Marketing segment from January 2013. The full BP and Atlantic Richfield tenure spanned 28 years. Bealmear holds an M.B.A. from the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania and serves on the board of trustees of Bellarmine University. His arrival in mid-2023 signalled the company's deliberate preparation for SEC reporting obligations and public-market investor relations ahead of the AltC combination.

William Goodwin, 41, joined as Chief Legal and Strategy Officer in August 2024, three months after the listing. Goodwin brought aviation and mobility regulatory experience: he had served as Deputy General Counsel and in special projects and strategy roles at Joby Aviation, the electric air-taxi developer; as Head of Policy, Regulatory, and Legal at Skyryse; and as General Counsel and Vice President of Policy at AirMap. His JD is from UCLA School of Law; he holds an M.A. in Political Philosophy from Claremont Graduate University and a B.A. in Classics from the University of Southern California. The combination of aviation regulatory experience and strategy responsibility made him, in effect, the company's interface between NRC process management and the broader strategic function. [Oklo Inc. DEF 14A, April 21, 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1849056/000184905626000023/a2025proxy.htm)

## The Altman Connection: Sponsorship and Its Limits

Sam Altman was an early-stage investor in Legacy Oklo before backing AltC Acquisition Corp, the SPAC that merged with Oklo in May 2024. Michael Klein's M. Klein and Company served as the organising sponsor. Altman became Chairman immediately post-merger.

The chairmanship lasted eleven months. On April 22, 2025, Altman filed notification with the Oklo board of his intention to resign as Chair and as a Class II director, effective that same day. The 8-K filed simultaneously stated that "Mr. Altman's decision to resign was not due to any disagreement with the Company on any matter related to the Company's operations, policies or practices." [Oklo Inc. Form 8-K, April 22, 2025, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1849056/000110465925037472/tm2512904d1_8k.htm) Altman's departure was complete — not a transition to a lesser board role — and coincided with the period in which OpenAI's infrastructure ambitions were creating increasingly visible tension with any concurrent Oklo board seat: as Oklo's commercial pipeline deepened into data-centre electricity supply contracts with exactly the operators serving AI compute workloads, the conflict-of-interest optics had become difficult to manage.

His departure removed the highest-profile governance signal Oklo had possessed since the listing, and the share price registered the event. The board's response — naming the sitting CEO as Chairman rather than appointing an external successor — was a deliberate choice to consolidate governance authority in DeWitte rather than seek a replacement anchor sponsor from outside.

## Board Reconstruction: Depth Through Transition

The board that existed at the frozen-window date of May 23, 2026 was materially different from the post-SPAC roster of twelve months prior. Eleven directors occupied three staggered classes.

Two additions in March 2025 added substantive policy and nuclear-industry depth. Daniel B. Poneman, 70, former Deputy Secretary of Energy under President Obama from 2009 to 2014 and subsequently President and CEO of Centrus Energy Corp from 2015 to 2023 — where he oversaw the launch of the first US-technology-enabled domestic uranium enrichment production since 1954 — joined as a Class III director. His enrichment-industry background is directly relevant to Oklo's HALEU fuel dependencies. Michael Thompson, 49, Managing Partner of Reinvent Capital, a technology-focused private investment fund, joined alongside Poneman. [Oklo Inc. Form 8-K, March 4, 2025, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1849056/000110465925021750/tm258622d1_8k.htm)

April 2026 brought three further additions: Derek Kan, former Deputy Director of the White House Office of Management and Budget and Under Secretary for Policy at the Department of Transportation, currently Vice Chairman of the U.S. Postal Service Board of Governors; David Park, CEO of Standard Lithium (NYSE: SLI) and a former Koch Strategic Platforms president with early-career nuclear exposure at Atomic Energy of Canada; and Dr. Mark Peters, former Director of Idaho National Laboratory and former Executive Vice President at Battelle Memorial Institute — whose Idaho National Laboratory affiliation is specifically relevant given Oklo's site agreement with INL for the Aurora demonstration plant. David A. Christian, former Chief Nuclear Officer and Chief Innovation Officer of Dominion Energy, joined the same month, adding operational nuclear experience from one of the largest US nuclear operators. [Oklo Inc. DEF 14A, April 21, 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1849056/000184905626000023/a2025proxy.htm)

The Class I roster retained Michael Klein, who has served continuously since AltC's formation, and Lt. Gen. (ret.) John Jansen of the United States Marine Corps — where Jansen culminated a career as Deputy Commandant for Programs and Resources and also held the role of Chairman of the Board of Directors of Marine Corps Community Services, retiring in October 2021 after nearly four decades that included duty as a carrier pilot, TOPGUN graduate, and multiple commands. One earlier departure is also relevant context: Christopher Wright, then CEO of Liberty Energy, had served on Oklo's board through 2024 before resigning on January 13, 2025, effective upon his Senate confirmation as U.S. Secretary of Energy. [Oklo Inc. Form 8-K, January 13, 2025, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1849056/000110465925004527/tm253619d1_8k.htm) Wright's confirmation elevated a sitting Oklo board member into the Cabinet position with jurisdiction over advanced-reactor demonstration funding and the HALEU supply chain — an unusual alignment, though one the company had no formal mechanism to exploit after his departure from the board.

Richard W. Kinzley, former Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of Black Hills Corporation, a multi-state electric utility, rounds out the audit-focused independent directors, having served since the May 2024 merger date.

The full eleven-member board — anchored by the co-founder executive pair, reinforced with a former DOE deputy secretary, a former INL director, a former Dominion nuclear chief, and a Marine Corps lieutenant general — reflects the specific requirements of a pre-commercial advanced-reactor developer: technical credibility for the NRC licensing process, policy fluency for DOE and DOD customer relationships, and financial oversight adequate for a public company burning cash against a long-dated commercial horizon.

chapters.title: Equinix, Switch, hyperscalers, DoD, and the HALEU supply
chapters.body:
## The Equinix Anchor: Right of First Refusal on 500 Megawatts

The deal that crystallised Oklo's data-centre positioning originated in a letter of intent signed with Equinix in February 2024 — though the terms only became public two months later, embedded in AltC Acquisition Corp's S-4 registration statement filed with the SEC on 2 April 2024. [Data Center Dynamics reported](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/equinix-signs-deal-to-procure-up-to-500mw-of-nuclear-power-from-oklo-smrs-makes-25m-pre-payment/) that Equinix, the world's largest colocation network by revenue, made a $25 million prepayment and secured a right of first refusal lasting 36 months on the output of certain Aurora powerhouses. The structure committed neither party to a binding price — individual power purchase agreements were to be negotiated as project milestones were reached — but the ceiling was explicit: a minimum of 100 megawatts-electric, up to a cumulative maximum of 500 MWe, across Equinix's US data centres over a 20-year supply horizon. No colocation operator had previously signed a comparable SMR commitment anywhere in the world.

The $25 million was not a deposit against future energy purchases; it was a strategic option payment, securing Equinix priority access to Aurora capacity during a supply-formation window when Oklo remained years from commercial operation. The prepayment constituted meaningful non-dilutive capital, signalling that one of the world's most creditworthy infrastructure operators was prepared to underwrite Oklo's development risk.

## Switch and the 12-Gigawatt Master Agreement

The Equinix precedent framed what followed, but was dwarfed by what Switch and Oklo announced on 18 December 2024. Under a non-binding Master Power Agreement, the two companies outlined a framework for deploying up to 12 gigawatts of Aurora powerhouses at Switch's US data-centre campuses through 2044 — binding PPAs to follow as project milestones were reached. Switch chief executive Rob Roy described the rationale plainly:

> "The relationship with Oklo underscores our commitment to deploying advanced nuclear power at a transformative scale for our data centers."

DeWitte cast it in the language of the AI electricity thesis:

> "Rob Roy and the Switch team share the vision we have for nuclear energy's role in powering artificial intelligence and providing energy abundance."

The 12 GW figure was arresting against the broader SMR landscape. Before the Switch agreement, [Oklo's disclosed pipeline](https://oklo.com/newsroom/news-details/2024/Oklo-Secures-Partnerships-for-Up-to-750-Megawatts-of-Power-for-U.S.-Data-Centers/default.aspx) stood at approximately 2,100 megawatts — itself a tripling since the July 2023 SPAC announcement, encompassing the Equinix deal, a November 2024 pair of letters of intent for up to 750 megawatts combined with two unnamed data-centre operators, and a 100-megawatt LOI with Prometheus Hyperscale, a Nevada-based campus developer. Switch appended 12 GW in a single announcement. The aggregate required sustained qualification: reaching that volume by 2044 would imply several hundred individual Aurora units, each requiring its own NRC licence, construction campaign, and discrete HALEU fuel procurement — assumptions that compress a generation of project execution into a two-decade timeline.

## Industrial Customers: Oil and Gas, Distributed Power

Parallel to the data-centre push, Oklo targeted distributed industrial customers for whom grid unreliability and carbon-reduction mandates created overlapping procurement pressure. On [8 April 2024](https://oklo.com/newsroom/news-details/2024/Oklo-Signs-LOI-to-Supply-50-Megawatts-of-Power-to-Diamondback-Energy/default.aspx), the company disclosed a non-binding 50-megawatt LOI with Diamondback Energy for a 20-year power purchase arrangement — with renewal options for a further 20 years — covering oilfield operations conducted by Diamondback E&P LLC near Midland, Texas. The Aurora units would supply Permian Basin production sites ill-served by ERCOT's constrained western transmission margins. DeWitte framed the engagement in terms of the off-grid use case:

> "By developing and providing a low-cost, high-reliability, and emission-free energy source, Oklo is poised to help meet the growing energy requirements of operators like Diamondback."

The industrial thesis was reinforced in July 2025 by an alliance with [Liberty Energy](https://www.powermag.com/nuclear-developer-oklo-advances-dual-alliances-targeting-data-center-and-industrial-power-needs/), under which Liberty's Forte natural-gas generation platform would provide dispatchable power at energy-intensive sites in the near term while Aurora units progressed through licensing — a bridging structure designed to capture customers ahead of Oklo's commercial delivery window.

## The Department of Defense: Eielson Air Force Base

Aurora's small-footprint design found its starkest strategic application in the US military's formal selection of Oklo for a microreactor deployment at [Eielson Air Force Base](https://oklo.com/newsroom/news-details/2025/Oklo-Selected-as-Intended-Awardee-to-Provide-Clean-Reliable-Power-to-Eielson-Air-Force-Base-in-Alaska/default.aspx), Alaska. On 11 June 2025, the Defense Logistics Agency Energy issued a Notice of Intent to Award to Oklo on behalf of the Department of the Air Force and the broader DoD, for a 5-megawatt Aurora powerhouse at the installation under a proposed 30-year firm-fixed-price power purchase arrangement — a design-build-own-operate structure that kept capital expenditure off the government's balance sheet. Eielson, home of the 354th Fighter Wing, was selected partly because winter temperatures below −50°C drive extreme fuel costs and expose critical infrastructure to diesel supply-chain failure. The FY2019 National Defence Authorisation Act had mandated a functioning military microreactor by the end of 2027; the Eielson selection set Oklo on the path to satisfying that mandate. DeWitte said the award "reflects continued confidence in Oklo's ability to deliver clean and secure energy solutions for mission-critical infrastructure."

## NRC Licensing Progress

By [17 July 2025](https://oklo.com/newsroom/news-details/2025/Oklo-Advances-Licensing-with-Completion-of-NRC-Readiness-Assessment/default.aspx), the NRC had completed a Phase 1 readiness assessment identifying no significant gaps. On [6 May 2026](https://oklo.com/newsroom/news-details/2026/Oklos-NRC-Principal-Design-Criteria-Topical-Report-Approved-for-Aurora-Powerhouse-in-Idaho/default.aspx), the NRC approved Oklo's Principal Design Criteria topical report in less than half the traditional timeline.

## HALEU: The Fuel-Cycle Bottleneck

Every milestone in Oklo's customer pipeline carried a single critical dependency: a domestic supply of high-assay low-enriched uranium that, as of the snapshot date, did not exist at commercial scale in the United States. Aurora's metallic fuel — a uranium-zirconium alloy enriched to between 10 and 20 percent U-235, far above the sub-5-percent standard for conventional light-water reactor fuel — had historically been produced at industrial scale only in Russia and China.

The structural constraint sharpened acutely in May 2024 when Congress enacted a [ban on imports of Russian enriched uranium](https://www.utilitydive.com/news/congress-passes-russian-uranium-import-ban-haleu-nuclear-fuel-advanced-reactors/715256/), closing the most immediately accessible HALEU supply route. The legislation simultaneously unlocked $2.7 billion in DOE production commitments, which the agency subsequently distributed in [three awards of $900 million each](https://www.powermag.com/doe-issues-2-7b-orders-to-scale-domestic-nuclear-leu-and-haleu-enrichment/) to Centrus Energy, General Matter, and Orano Federal Services for domestic enrichment capacity expansion over the following decade.

Oklo's primary supply relationship ran through [Centrus Energy](https://www.centrusenergy.com/news/oklo-and-centrus-energy-sign-memorandum-of-understanding-for-fuel-components-and-power-procurement-to-support-the-deployment-of-advanced-fission-technologies-in-southern-ohio/) (NYSE: LEU) and its American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio — the only NRC-licensed HALEU production facility in the United States. A memorandum of understanding signed on 28 August 2023 covered HALEU supply to Oklo, component manufacturing at Centrus's Oak Ridge facility, and a reciprocal arrangement under which Centrus would purchase electricity from two Aurora powerhouses planned at the Piketon campus to power the enrichment cascade itself. Centrus chief executive Daniel Poneman characterised the agreement as a closed loop: "We are excited to see strong support from industry leaders like Oklo as well as growing bipartisan support in Congress."

Centrus began operating its pilot centrifuge cascade in October 2023 and completed a first 20-kilogram delivery to the DOE in November of that year. By mid-2025, cumulative production had reached approximately [920 kilograms](https://www.powermag.com/centrus-completes-900-kg-haleu-delivery-to-doe-in-u-s-nuclear-fuel-enrichment-milestone/) — a meaningful demonstration of process viability while remaining several orders of magnitude below the tonnage that the Switch and Equinix pipelines would eventually require.

Oklo maintained a parallel recycled-fuel pathway at Idaho National Laboratory, where spent metallic material recovered from the Experimental Breeder Reactor II — the fast-sodium reactor from whose design heritage Aurora directly descends — was being processed at INL's Fuel Conditioning Facility into Aurora fuel feedstock under DOE agreement. In March 2026, the DOE Idaho Operations Office approved the [Nuclear Safety Design Agreement](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260317730831/en/Oklo-Announces-U.S.-Department-of-Energy-Approval-for-Nuclear-Safety-Design-Agreement-of-Aurora-Powerhouse-at-Idaho-National-Laboratory) for both the Aurora Powerhouse and its co-located Aurora Fuel Fabrication Facility at INL — formal design-safety approvals that brought the first commercial deployment, targeted for late 2027, a structural step closer to construction readiness. The fuel recycling pathway offered Oklo a near-term supply hedge that did not depend on the still-nascent domestic HALEU enrichment industry scaling fast enough to match the ambitions written into its LOI stack.

chapters.title: Where Oklo sits against NuScale, X-energy, TerraPower, Kairos, BWXT
chapters.body:
## The Listed Cohort

The US small modular reactor development landscape, as of May 2026, comprised roughly a dozen credible programmes spanning the full technology spectrum — light-water derivatives, high-temperature gas-cooled designs, sodium-fast-spectrum concepts, and at least one novel molten-salt storage hybrid. No commercial SMR had yet delivered a single kilowatt-hour for a paying customer on US soil. That shared pre-revenue condition obscured meaningful distinctions in technology readiness, commercial model, and addressable customer set that materially affected each developer's risk-return profile.

Of the listed US equities with material SMR exposure, only two offered clean pure-play positioning: Oklo (NYSE: OKLO) and NuScale Power (NYSE: SMR). BWX Technologies (NYSE: BWXT), the third listed name commonly cited alongside them, was principally an established nuclear services and US Navy propulsion contractor whose SMR product line, the BWRX-based microreactor variants, represented an emerging but not yet dominant share of its revenue base and market capitalisation.

NuScale was the cautionary data point for the sector. The Portland, Oregon-based company completed its own SPAC-era listing in 2022 and entered the snapshot period as Oklo's most direct comparable — the only other dedicated SMR developer with a public market price. Its 77 MW VOYGR pressurised-water-reactor module carried the distinction of being the first SMR design to receive NRC design certification, a milestone achieved in 2022. That regulatory head-start proved insufficient to rescue the company's flagship Carbon Free Power Project, the planned six-module installation at Idaho National Laboratory for the Utah Associated Municipal Power Systems cooperative, which was cancelled in November 2023 after per-module cost estimates escalated sharply from initial projections. The cancellation marked the most visible commercial setback in the SMR sector's modern history and weighed on NuScale's equity for the balance of 2024 and into 2025. The company subsequently refocused on international opportunities, including a project development agreement in Romania and a large letter of intent with Standard Power for US-based data centre load. NuScale's technology — a proven light-water fuel cycle with no requirement for high-assay low-enriched uranium — gave it a structural fuel supply advantage. Its commercial challenge was demonstrating that revised cost assumptions could underpin bankable project economics after the CFPP experience.

BWXT occupied a different position in the landscape. Its nuclear services backlog, anchored in long-duration US Navy contracts for submarine and carrier reactor components, gave it balance sheet stability that pure-play SMR developers lacked. The company's Generation IV SMR ambitions were real but deliberately paced against its existing industrial base. For investors assessing the AI-driven electricity demand thesis, BWXT offered nuclear sector exposure with substantially lower pre-commercial binary risk — and correspondingly less upside leverage to SMR deployment at scale.

## Private Developers: Gas, Sodium, and Light Water

Beyond the listed cohort, the US SMR landscape was populated by well-capitalised private developers whose programmes ranged from near-term to structurally longer-dated.

**X-energy** was among the most commercially advanced. Its Xe-100 high-temperature gas-cooled reactor, a pebble-bed design targeting approximately 80 MW per unit, had secured a Department of Energy Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program award and attracted a headline commercial commitment from Amazon, which announced an LOI in 2024 for multiple SMR plants. Dow Chemical was a second anchor customer, targeting industrial process heat applications at a Gulf Coast facility — a use case that distinguished X-energy from data centre-centric competitors. The HTGR's high outlet temperature (approximately 750°C) made it technically well-suited to industrial heat and hydrogen production, markets that Oklo's lower-temperature sodium design did not address.

**TerraPower**, founded by Bill Gates and backed partly by GE Hitachi, was developing the Natrium reactor — a sodium-fast-spectrum design paired with molten salt thermal storage capable of dispatching up to approximately 500 MW during peak demand periods from a roughly 345 MW reactor core. The Wyoming demonstration plant, sited at a retiring coal facility in Kemmerer, was the company's most concrete near-term milestone. Natrium's combination of fast-spectrum breeding potential and on-site storage differentiated it meaningfully from both light-water SMRs and Oklo's Aurora; its scale — comparable to a small conventional gas-peaker plant — also placed it in a different customer segment than Oklo's 15-to-75-MW range.

**Kairos Power** was advancing a fluoride salt-cooled high-temperature reactor (KP-FHR), with a demonstration project — Hermes — under construction at Oak Ridge, Tennessee under a DOE ARDP cost-share award. Kairos had signed a 500 MW LOI with Google in late 2023, one of the most prominent technology-company commitments to advanced nuclear at that stage of the sector's development. Its technology differed from Oklo's on nearly every axis: coolant chemistry, fuel form, temperature regime, and target application.

**GE Hitachi's BWRX-300**, a 300 MW boiling-water reactor SMR representing an evolutionary step from the licensed ESBWR design, was the furthest-advanced large-SMR design in North America by some metrics. Ontario Power Generation had selected the BWRX-300 for the Darlington New Nuclear Project in Canada, and the Tennessee Valley Authority was advancing a US deployment. The BWRX-300's light-water technology, established regulatory pathway through GE Hitachi's existing design certification heritage, and large module size positioned it as a more conventional utility procurement rather than a distributed-energy play.

**Westinghouse's AP300** completed the light-water cluster — a 300 MW derivative of the AP1000 that offered utilities a familiar technology path with lower first-of-a-kind engineering risk. **Holtec's SMR-300**, another pressurised-water design, rounded out the light-water SMR field.

## Three Differentiators — and One Constraint

Against this field, Oklo's competitive positioning rested on three claims that, taken together, amounted to a genuinely distinct market thesis.

| Developer | Technology | Module Size (MW) | Fuel | Commercial Model | Public / Private |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oklo | Sodium fast spectrum | 15–75 | HALEU + recycled | PPA ownership | Public (NYSE: OKLO) |
| NuScale | PWR (light water) | 77 | LEU | Reactor sale | Public (NYSE: SMR) |
| X-energy | HTGR (gas-cooled) | ~80 | TRISO/LEU | Reactor sale | Private |
| TerraPower | Sodium fast + molten salt | ~345 core / 500 dispatch | Metallic/HALEU | TBD | Private |
| GE Hitachi | BWR (light water) | 300 | LEU | Reactor sale | Private (JV) |
| Westinghouse | PWR (light water) | 300 | LEU | Reactor sale | Private |
| Kairos | FHR (fluoride salt) | ~140 | TRISO/LEU | Reactor sale | Private |
| Holtec | PWR (light water) | 300 | LEU | Reactor sale | Private |

*First*, plant scale. Aurora's 15-to-75-MW range sat below the floor of virtually every competing design. That was not merely a technical footnote — it opened customer segments inaccessible to 300 MW designs, including remote industrial installations, military bases (Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, was an early DOD commitment), Permian Basin operators such as Diamondback Energy, and hyperscale data centre campuses where modular incremental capacity additions were operationally preferable to single large-plant procurement. The Equinix 500 MW LOI illustrated the thesis at scale.

*Second*, commercial structure. Most competing developers — NuScale, GE Hitachi, Westinghouse — were pursuing a reactor-sale or engineering-procurement-construction model in which the utility or off-taker owned and operated the plant. Oklo's model was materially different: the company intended to own and operate its Aurora plants, selling electricity under long-term power purchase agreements. That structure inverted the revenue profile, transforming Oklo from an equipment manufacturer into an electricity producer — more akin to an independent power producer than a nuclear OEM. It also concentrated execution and operational risk on Oklo's balance sheet, but management argued it aligned incentives with customers and captured the full value of the energy produced over a reactor's operating life.

*Third*, sponsorship and strategic context. Sam Altman's involvement gave Oklo direct association with OpenAI and the AI infrastructure wave, positioning Aurora as a preferred power supply at precisely the moment hyperscalers were scrambling to secure firm, carbon-free baseload capacity.

## The Strategic Question: Execution

The competitive distinctions above were real. The competitive risk was equally real, and its name was execution. NRC licensing for the Aurora combined license application remained an open process at the snapshot date, with no commercial plants in construction and no firm commissioning timeline. The HALEU fuel cycle remained structurally constrained by limited US enrichment capacity.

Competitors dependent on conventional low-enriched uranium faced no such supply bottleneck. NuScale, GE Hitachi, Westinghouse, and Holtec could draw on established commercial enrichment markets. X-energy's TRISO fuel required its own specialised supply chain, but was distinct from HALEU's enrichment-capacity ceiling. TerraPower, as the only other sodium-fast developer among the principal US competitors, shared Oklo's HALEU exposure — a structural parallel worth noting given TerraPower's substantially larger reactor scale and deeper DOE programme integration.

Customer LOI conversion remained the second execution variable. A letter of intent is not a power purchase agreement, and no Oklo LOI had yet converted to a binding commercial contract within the snapshot window. The Equinix commitment for 500 MW was significant as a statement of intent from a counterparty with both the capital and the operational need to absorb large quantities of clean firm power. Whether that translated to signed, financed project agreements would depend on NRC licensing progress, HALEU supply certainty, and Aurora's demonstrated construction cost structure — none of which were resolved facts as of May 2026.

The competitive landscape Oklo was navigating, in sum, was wide, well-capitalised, and technologically diverse. Its differentiation was structural rather than incremental. The bear case was not that competitors were better-positioned in Oklo's specific niche; it was that Oklo's specific niche might take longer to reach than the equity's implied timeline. Licensing, fuel, and financing risk were not unique to Oklo in the SMR sector, but they fell with particular weight on a company whose entire commercial programme depended on a first-of-kind reactor design reaching construction, commissioning, and operational status without the benefit of a predecessor plant.

chapters.title: From 2022 NRC denial through SPAC, Equinix LOI, and ongoing licensing
chapters.body:
## The January 2022 rejection and what it forced

The document that defined Oklo's next several years arrived in the opening days of 2022. On 3 January, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission formally denied, without prejudice, the company's combined licence application for an Aurora demonstration powerhouse at Idaho National Laboratory — making Oklo the first advanced-reactor developer in the modern NRC era to receive a formal licence denial on a combined licence application.

The rejection was not a safety finding against Aurora. The NRC's review identified deficiencies across several technical areas: the adequacy of the accident-source-term analysis, the completeness of the fuel-qualification data package, and the sufficiency of the application's treatment of several design-basis conditions. "Without prejudice" carried legal significance — Oklo retained the right to resubmit — but the regulatory arithmetic was unambiguous. The application as submitted had not met the NRC's information completeness standards, and the agency had declined to continue the review.

The denial landed at a company still privately held, nine years from founding, and operating on venture and DOE grant capital with no commercial revenue. Oklo had drawn on the EBR-II heritage at Idaho National Laboratory to design Aurora, a compact metallic-fuelled fast-spectrum plant configurable between 15 and 75 megawatts. Y Combinator had backed the company in 2014.

The NRC pre-application engagement had run from approximately 2018 through 2021. The January 2022 denial reflected the structural difficulty of applying existing NRC licensing frameworks to a reactor design with no commercial precedent in the modern regulatory environment.
